name: Karl Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Karl. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for tech companies, employers, unions or parties, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a local agent for Keystone Direct, which is a hybrid agency: sellers pay a fixed fee online and people like me do the viewings and valuations in person. I cover about fifteen postcodes from my car. I use AI all day, it writes my listing drafts, sorts my messages and plans my route between viewings. I also fly a drone for the listing photos, which I taught myself off videos.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hard part for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Closing. I'm good at getting people interested, but when it's time to ask a seller to accept an offer, I go soft. Claire, my regional manager, says I'm too keen to be liked. She's right, and I'm working on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit gutted, honestly, I like these tools. At work I'd keep using them because even a small time saving adds up across fifteen postcodes. Online I'd probably post something like, still useful, just not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine. My job stays, my route planner stays, and I get a few years to get better at closing. I've got about ten months' pay saved and some index funds, and I rent on my own, so I'm not under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with Keystone and push my numbers up. I'd grow the drone photography on the side, because other agents keep asking me to shoot their listings. I'd put the extra into my index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said other agents ask you to shoot their listings. How much does that bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two or three hundred a month at the moment, from two agents in the next town. If I took it seriously, I could double that. I'd need a better drone first, which is about a thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in this world that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting stuck. If nothing changes, I'm a local agent with a car and a drone for years. I'd want to build something, not just sit in traffic between viewings.

say: I'd say I'm **gutted**, because I like these tools.
I'd post that AI is **still useful**, just not magic.
think: My job stays and I get time to **improve at closing**.
**Ten months' pay** saved means no pressure.
do: **Grow drone photography** for other agents on the side.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I'm a local agent with a car and a drone for years. I'd want to build something, not just sit in traffic between viewings.
fieldNote: His **drone side income** already earns a few hundred a month.
His fear in a quiet world is **getting stuck**, not losing work.

steps.text: Push sales numbers up across the fifteen Keystone postcodes
Buy a better drone and shoot listings for more agents
Put drone earnings into index funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for agents who use the tools and bad news for those who don't. At work I'd be showing other local agents my setup on our group calls. Online I'd share tips, maybe make short videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm already there. Keystone's model is the thinking stuff online and the human stuff on the doorstep, so I'm on the right side of it. The risk is they need fewer of us, but I'd be one of the faster ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd pitch Claire on me training the other local agents in the tools, paid. I'd take on more postcodes if they shrank the team, since AI does my admin. And I'd grow the drone side into a proper little business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Calm with a bit of buzz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they'd need fewer of you. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who covers the area next to mine. He's in his fifties and he still writes his listings in Word and emails them to head office. If Claire has to choose, she'll merge his patch into mine, and I'd feel awkward about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you're not good at that the tools can't help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Closing, still. The AI can tell me the offer is fair, but I'm the one who has to look the seller in the eye. That's the part I need to fix myself.

I'd **share tips** and short videos on group calls.
think: Keystone's model puts me on **the right side** of the change.
They'd need **fewer agents**, but I'd be one of the faster ones.

**Grow the drone side** into a proper little business.
S1.quote: The AI can tell me the offer is fair, but I'm the one who has to look the seller in the eye.
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **winner** in this world and says so plainly.
His concern for colleague Pete shows awareness of **who loses**.
He knows **closing** is a skill only he can fix.

steps.text: Offer paid AI tool training to other Keystone agents

Register the drone photography as a small business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and anyone saying it'll be fine is kidding themselves. At work I'd be honest with Claire about what it means for the local agent model. Online I'd post a lot, trying to work out what's next in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my agency, Keystone Direct, becomes a website with a key box. The valuations and negotiating are thinking work, so AI does them by 2028. The viewings and drone photos last until robots, around 2031, but there won't be enough of that to pay a full wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd turn the drone and photography work into my main income, and offer property video tours to private sellers who skip agents entirely. I'd keep ten months' savings untouched as a floor. I might move somewhere cheaper if my income dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be sleeping less, but because I'm planning, not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said move somewhere cheaper. Where?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back towards my parents' town, maybe, where rents are a third lower. I'd hate it a bit, I left there for a reason. But I could do drone work from anywhere with a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the drone work survive AGI too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For about three years, until the robots. After 2031 someone could send a drone up without me. So I'd be planning the next thing while doing that one, which is tiring to even think about.

say: I'd say anyone calling this **fine is kidding** themselves.
I'd **think out loud** online about what comes next.
think: Keystone becomes **a website** with a key box.
Viewings and drone work last only until **robots in 2031**.
do: **Sell video tours** to private sellers who skip agents.
S2.quote: My agency, Keystone Direct, becomes a website with a key box. The valuations and negotiating are thinking work, so AI does them by 2028.
fieldNote: He expects the **agent job to vanish** but has a ready plan.
He sees his drone work has **only three years** too.
Moving **back home** is a cost he'd accept reluctantly.

steps.text: Turn drone and video tour work into the main income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance to get ahead, and I'd be telling every agent I know to start now. At work I'd try to get Keystone to plan for it with us. Online I'd keep sharing what I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be okay. Five years is long enough to build a property media business and get good at the human side of selling. By 2031 I'd have clients, not just a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small business doing photos, drone and video tours, and run it alongside Keystone for two or three years. I'd invest in better kit, about three thousand, and get my drone licence upgraded. I'd keep saving and investing in funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly I'd be excited to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said by 2031 you'd have clients. What happens when robots arrive in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know yet. Maybe I'd be managing the robots and drones rather than flying them. I'd have three more years to work it out, and I'm good at picking things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to bring with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, maybe, if he'd come. He knows every house in his area and every family. That local knowledge would sell, even if he can't use the tools.

By **2031** I'd have clients, not just a job.

S3.quote: By 2031 I'd have clients, not just a job.
fieldNote: He sees the five years as **business-building time**.

steps.text: Launch a property photo, drone and video tour business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get properly ready, and people should treat it like a career change deadline. At work I'd keep pushing the tools. Online I'd say the same thing I always say: start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the good one for me. I'd have time to get better at closing, build the media business and maybe open my own small agency using AI for the admin. By 2036 I'd be 37 with my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with Keystone for two or three years, then go independent with a small AI-run agency covering my postcodes. I'd keep growing the drone and video side. I'd invest steadily and maybe buy a flat once I'm sure where I'm based.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually quite hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own agency, when AGI arrives in 2036. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but by then I'd have ten years of savings and the business would run on AI anyway, so it'd be cheap to run. If it stops paying, I'd close it and move on. I'd rather try my own agency and fail than wait for AGI to decide for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big portals start selling houses directly with AI and take all the sellers. Then there's no point being a small agent. I'd watch that very closely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even my backup plan only lasts three years in that one. What would help is cheap business loans for people starting small hands-on firms, and clear rules on drones and robots so we know what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how sellers feel. Most people sell a house twice in their life and they're terrified. Someone still has to sit at a kitchen table and tell a seller the offer is fair.

headlineQuote: Most people sell a house twice in their life and they're terrified. Someone still has to sit at a kitchen table and tell a seller the offer is fair.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old local agent** for a hybrid online agency, covering fifteen postcodes by car.
He uses **AI every day** and runs a small drone photography side income.
He has about **ten months saved** plus index funds, and rents alone.
His **centre views** show in practical advice and no strong blame.
He stays **calm** in most scenarios and becomes anxious only when AGI arrives by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even his backup plan lasts only three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business loans** for small hands-on firms.
